item.title: Altered Intrinsic Brain Network Organization in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Differential Associations with Pain Sensitivity and Perceived Stress.
item.description:
Neuroimmunomodulation
INTRODUCTION: The persistence of abdominal pain and related gastrointestinal symptoms despite disease remission suggests that inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) may involve central alterations that extend beyond periods of active intestinal inflammation. Yet, intrinsic brain network organization in ulcerative colitis (UC) remains insufficiently characterized, particularly in relation to factors relevant to symptom persistence, such as pain sensitivity and chronic stress burden. We therefore investigated resting-state functional connectivity (FC) within the default mode network (DMN) and salience network in UC and examined associations with heat pain thresholds and perceived chronic stress. METHODS: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 17 female patients with UC and 19 female healthy controls (HC) were analyzed using group-level independent component analysis. FC differences within the identified DMN and salience network components were assessed in a priori defined regions of interest implicated in interoceptive and affective pain-related processing. Associations between altered FC and heat pain thresholds as well as perceived chronic stress were examined. RESULTS: Patients with UC differed from HC in the intrinsic organization of both the DMN and salience network. DMN alterations included increased FC of the posterior insula and medial superior frontal gyrus, alongside decreased FC of the dorsolateral superior frontal gyrus. Salience network alterations involved increased FC of the anterior insula, midcingulate cortex, and orbital inferior frontal gyrus. In UC, stronger FC of the anterior insula and orbital inferior frontal gyrus within the salience network was associated with lower heat pain thresholds, corresponding to greater experimental pain sensitivity. These associations were absent in HC. Connectivity of the orbital inferior frontal gyrus was additionally associated with perceived chronic stress in HC, but not in UC. CONCLUSION: UC is characterized by altered intrinsic organization of brain networks central to interoceptive and affective pain-related processing. The association between stronger salience network connectivity and greater experimental pain sensitivity suggests that central network alterations may be involved in pain-related mechanisms beyond acute intestinal inflammation. These findings highlight the potential clinical relevance of considering central pain mechanisms alongside peripheral inflammation to better understand persistent pain in IBD.

item.title: Brain cycle flexibility and behavioral association
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.

item.title: Resting-State Imaging of Vestibular Migraine:Integrative Insights from Amplitude,Homogeneity,and Functional Connection.
item.description:
Zhongguo yi xue ke xue yuan xue bao. Acta Academiae Medicinae Sinicae
Vestibular migraine (VM) represents a prevalent central vestibular disorder characterized by episodic vertigo and migraine attacks,yet its neuropathological basis remains poorly understood.Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging has emerged as a valuable investigative tool for identifying central network dysfunction in VM,given its sensitivity in detecting spontaneous brain activity.Drawing on seed-based functional connectivity studies and measures including amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,and regional homogeneity,this review examines aberrant spontaneous activity in VM patients across the thalamus,cerebellum,frontoparietal cortex,and insula.Key pathological circuits include disrupted vestibular-thalamo-cortical projections,dysregulated pain-emotion processing networks,and compensatory recruitment of visual-spatial attention and motor pathways.These findings furnish important neuroimaging evidence for understanding the pathophysiology and identifying the potential diagnostic and therapeutic biomarkers for VM.

item.title: Adiposity in Adolescence has Detrimental Effects on Developing Brain Structures and Organization, Communication, and Controllability of Resting-State Networks
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Adiposity in adolescence can have detrimental effects on neural maturation, and is associated with incompletely understood alterations in brain structures and circuits. To address this important knowledge gap, N = 3,341 youth from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) two-year follow-up cohort (median(IQR) age = 12.0(1.1) years; 51.0% females), with structural MRI and resting-state fMRI were studied. Topological properties reflecting network strength, resilience, efficiency and modularity, information transfer, regional feedback costs associated with controllability of network dynamics, and morphometric characteristics were examined as a function of body mass index (BMI), body roundness index (BRI), overweight, obesity, and persistent excess BMI (across assessments). Youth who slept less, spent more time on electronic devices, were Hispanic and/or from lower-income families had higher BMI/BRI (β = 0.07–4.95, 95%CI=[0.03,7.05]), and higher odds of overweight or obesity (aOR = 1.01–1.72, 95%CI=[1.01,2.28]). Higher BMI/BRI, overweight, obesity and/or persistent excess BMI were associated with weaker and less resilient networks supporting decision-making, control, emotional regulation, reward processing and social function (β=-0.11 to -0.01, CI=[-0.16,-0.01]), and more topologically fragile thalamus and basal ganglia (β = 0.05–0.10, CI=[0.01,0.14], p < 0.03). They were also associated with lower control costs in cognitive and topological hubs (including the precuneus and prefrontal regions) that play central roles in regulating brain dynamics, aberrant information transfer in limbic, frontoparietal, salience, somatomotor and cerebellar regions, and lower thickness and/or volume of distributed (including prefrontal) regions, and functional hubs (β=-0.14 to -0.02, CI=[-0.18,-0.01]). Thus, adiposity in adolescence is associated with widespread structural and alterations of brain networks supporting developing cognitive processes, and fundamental mechanisms that control these networks’ dynamics.

item.title: Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing during Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.
item.description:
eNeuro
Language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation. Here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations. We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels. In contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components. These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties.Significance statement Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages. Using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level. These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.

item.title: Exploring prefrontal mitochondrial metabolism and its coupling with hemoxygenation as biomarkers for cognition and psychopathology: A pilot fNIRS study.
item.description:
Neuroimmunomodulation
Cerebral mitochondrial dysregulation and altered neurometabolic coupling have been implicated across psychiatric and neurocognitive disorders. However, in vivo human data assessing these mechanisms within a transdiagnostic framework remain limited. We investigated left frontopolar mitochondrial metabolism, blood oxygenation, and their coupling at rest and during cognitive tasks in relation to general psychopathology (p) and general cognition (g). In a transdiagnostic sample of 65 adults (n=50 included after quality control), changes in mitochondrial metabolism (Δ[oxCCO]) and blood oxygenation (Δ[HbD]) were measured at the left frontal pole (Fp1) using single-channel broadband functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Three mitochondrial-hemoxygenation coupling indices were computed: relative power (rPwr), relative cost (rCst) and intraindividual distance correlation. Outcomes included composite factors for general psychopathology (p, derived from validated self-report questionnaires) and general cognition (g, derived from four cognitive tasks). Primary confirmatory hypotheses were not confirmed: task-evoked mitochondrial metabolism and interindividual coupling markers (rPwr, rCst) showed no significant associations with p or g, nor did they differentiate diagnostic status groups (p > 0.05). In exploratory analyses, a higher intraindividual task-evoked mitochondrial-hemoxygenation correlation was associated with higher g (r = 0.44, p = 0.008; n = 35). Conversely, higher resting-state Δ[oxCCO] and Δ[HbD] were associated with lower g (r = -0.58 and r = -0.55, both p ≤ 0.001; n = 31). Associations with general psychopathology were not statistically significant. While primary confirmatory hypotheses were rejected, exploratory findings provide preliminary evidence that prefrontal mitochondrial-hemoxygenation coupling (both at rest and during cognitive engagement) is relevant to cognitive functioning. Given the pilot nature and data loss constraints, this non-invasive broadband fNIRS approach warrants validation in larger, adequately powered confirmatory studies.

item.title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype-expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.
item.description:
Nature biomedical engineering
Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological-environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure-function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic-exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

item.title: Whole-Brain Dynamics and Cognitive Flexibility in Level 1 ASD: An HMM-Based Approach.
item.description:
Journal of autism and developmental disorders
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by differences in cognitive flexibility, which are closely associated with restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB). However, the dynamic brain network mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood. This study investigated the neural correlates of cognitive flexibility difficulties in ASD by analyzing dynamic brain network features and explored their potential as diagnostic biomarkers. We applied hidden Markov models (HMMs) to resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data to characterize dynamic brain network states in children with ASD (n = 69) and typically developing (TD) children (n = 50). Cognitive flexibility was assessed using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF). An independent ABIDE II dataset was used for external validation. Machine learning models evaluated the diagnostic utility of behavioral and neuroimaging markers. Children with ASD showed atypical brain network dynamics, specifically a reduced brain state switching rate (p < 0.01) and asymmetric activation of the frontoparietal network (FPN). These alterations were significantly associated with cognitive flexibility difficulties and RRB severity in the ASD group (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q < 0.05) and generalized to the independent sample. Combining cognitive flexibility scores with brain state switching rates yielded high diagnostic accuracy (internal AUC: 0.897 (95% CI 0.812-0.963); external AUC: 0.869 (95% CI 0.781-0.943)). This study provides novel insights into the dynamic neural mechanisms underlying cognitive flexibility differences in ASD. The findings support combined behavioral and neuroimaging biomarkers for improving ASD diagnosis and lay the groundwork for individualized intervention research.

item.title: Combined Neuromelanin-Sensitive and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Links Midbrain Dopaminergic Dysfunction to Connectome Architecture in First-Episode, Medication-Naïve Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Accumulating evidence implicates dopaminergic dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet direct evidence of such dysfunction and of its altered coupling with the functional connectome remains limited. Methods Using neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) and resting-state fMRI, we examined differences in substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area NM-MRI signal (NMSSN/VTA ) between first-episode, medication-naïve MDD patients (n = 112) and healthy controls (HC; n = 230). Network-based statistics (NBS) assessed MDD-related alterations in NMSSN/VTA -functional connectivity (FC) coupling. Spatial correspondence analyses examined the spatial convergence of these coupling alterations with normative dopaminergic molecular maps and anhedonia-related connectome patterns in MDD. Results Patients with MDD showed lower NMSSN/VTA , with more pronounced reductions in lateral and rostral regions. NBS identified a widespread component with altered NMSSN/VTA -FC coupling in MDD, characterized predominantly by higher slopes across attention, control, sensory, and medial temporal systems and lower slopes involving limbic-striatal and default-mode connections. Network-level analysis further identified a diagnosis-dependent NMSSN/VTA -striatal-limbic connectivity relationship, with lower NMSSN/VTA associated with higher FC in MDD. Spatially, these coupling alterations converged with dopaminergic molecular architecture, showing negative correspondence with normative dopaminergic receptor and transporter distributions and positive correspondence with the anticipatory-pleasure-related connectome pattern in MDD. Conclusions These findings provide in vivo evidence of midbrain dopaminergic dysfunction and widespread disruption of dopaminergic-connectome coupling in MDD, with these coupling alterations spatially converging with anhedonia-related connectome organization. Together, these findings advance our understanding of the role of dopaminergic dysfunction in the pathophysiology of MDD.

item.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory.
item.description:
eLife
Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity-brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay-in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal-neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

item.title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

item.title: Discourse coherence in first-episode psychosis and depression: shared referential alterations and links to cortical hierarchy
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Disrupted discourse coherence is documented in psychosis, but whether depression shows similar alterations, and how these relate to cortical hierarchical organization, remains unclear. This is the first study to examine conceptual and referential dimensions of coherence and their associations with cortical hierarchy across first-episode psychosis and depression. We analysed spontaneous speech from 85 German speakers (29 controls, 28 with first-episode psychosis, 28 with first-episode depression), of whom 80 underwent resting-state fMRI. Using large-model embeddings, automated coreference resolution, and graph-theoretical measures, we quantified conceptual relations (i.e., how ideas are linked) and referential relations (i.e., how entities are introduced and maintained), and related them to gradient dispersion between networks and within the semantic-associative network. Both clinical groups showed reduced referential continuity, and less small-world organization of conceptual content than controls, whereas differences in local semantic similarity depended on diagnosis and language model. Negative symptom severity was associated with altered conceptual and referential relations. Between-network gradient dispersion did not differ between groups. However, after controlling for diagnosis, individual variation in gradient organization was associated with distinct conceptual and referential relations. Visual-default mode network dispersion was associated with conceptual network organization, while somatomotor-default mode network dispersion was associated with local conceptual and referential coherence. Dispersion within the semantic-associative network was linked with topic reorganization. These findings identify reduced referential continuity as a shared, automatically measurable speech alteration across early psychosis and depression, linked to negative symptoms and cortical hierarchy, and support developing scalable speech-based markers for transdiagnostic assessment and differential diagnosis.

item.title: Connectome Harmonic Analysis at 7 Tesla Reveals Selective Reorganization of Large-Scale Cortical Dynamics in Adult Users of Cannabis.
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Cannabis exposure is associated with altered functional connectivity, cognitive impairment, and psychosis-spectrum risk, but the systems-level principles through which it reshapes large-scale brain organization remain poorly understood. Connectome Harmonic Analysis (CHA), a spectral graph-theoretic framework, characterizes the intrinsic spatial modes governing cortical communication. We investigated whether cannabis use alters low-frequency connectome harmonics using ultra-high-field 7 Tesla MRI. Methods Resting-state fMRI and high angular resolution diffusion data from the Human Connectome Project 7T cohort were used for Connectome Harmonic Analysis in 81 cannabis users (CU) and 81 matched non-users (NU). BOLD activity was projected onto the first 200 connectome harmonics; group differences in harmonic power were assessed with independent-samples t-tests and FDR correction, and significant harmonics were anatomically localized using the HCP multimodal parcellation atlas. Results Cannabis users exhibited significantly increased power in a single low-frequency connectome harmonic (k = 6; λ₆ = 0.01144; t ≈ 4.19; p_FDR = 7.21 × 10⁻³; Cohen’s d = 0.659), reflecting approximately 44% greater normalized power than non-users; no higher-frequency harmonics survived correction. This harmonic localized to a distributed frontoparietal–sensorimotor network spanning bilateral premotor, supplementary motor, and superior parietal cortex, intraparietal sulcus, and supramarginal gyrus, and did not correlate with cannabis clinical exposure variables (age at onset, duration, frequency, or abuse/dependence diagnosis; all ρ < 0.09, p > 0.44). Behavioral correlation analyses revealed nominal, domain-specific associations — slower working memory reaction time across the cohort (ρ = +0.18, p = 0.026), greater ADHD symptom burden (ρ = +0.23, p = 0.041) and extraversion (ρ = +0.25, p = 0.026) in cannabis users, and lower theory-of-mind accuracy in non-users (ρ = −0.23, p = 0.042) — though standard cognitive composites were null and no association survived FDR correction. Conclusions Cannabis use is associated with selective amplification of a low-frequency connectome harmonic subserving frontoparietal–sensorimotor integration, suggesting that cannabis exposure alters the brain’s intrinsic dynamical architecture at the level of macroscale eigenmodes rather than isolated regional circuits. Connectome harmonics may thus provide a systems-level biomarker linking cannabinoid neurobiology to cortical coordination relevant to psychosis vulnerability, predictive processing abnormalities, and network dysregulation in psychiatric illness.

item.title: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface training for upper-limb rehabilitation after subacute stroke: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
item.description:
PloS one
Objective To determine whether motor imagery (MI) based brain-computer interface (BCI) training improves upper-limb motor function in patients with subacute stroke compared with a high-fidelity sham-BCI control, and to explore accompanying structural and resting-state functional MRI changes. Method In this participant-blinded randomized controlled trial, 32 patients with subacute stroke were randomized to a MI-based BCI group or a high-fidelity BCI sham-control group (n = 16 each). Both groups received dose-matched training (30 min/session, 5 sessions/week for 4 weeks) in addition to standard rehabilitation. Upper-limb motor outcomes were assessed using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE; primary outcome), Wolf Motor Function Test (WMFT), Motor Assessment Scale (MAS), and Modified Barthel Index (MBI). Structural MRI and resting-state functional MRI were acquired at baseline and post-intervention to assess gray matter volume (GMV) and functional connectivity (FC). Results Both groups showed significant improvement after the intervention. Compared with the sham-control group, the MI-based BCI group demonstrated greater gains in FMA-UE and secondary motor outcomes (WMFT and MAS), whereas the difference in MBI was not statistically significant. Voxel-based morphometry revealed a within-group increase in GMV in the contralesional supplementary motor area (SMA) in the MI-based BCI group; however, no significant between-group GMV difference was observed. The MI-based BCI group also exhibited increased resting-state FC between the SMA and the ipsilesional cerebellar lobule IX and fusiform gyrus. Changes in FC were associated with improvements in FMA-UE, WMFT, and MBI, but not MAS. Conclusion Compared with a high-fidelity sham-control group, MI-based BCI group training was associated with greater upper-limb motor recovery in patients with subacute stroke, accompanied by changes in structural and functional neuroimaging measures involving motor-related regions and connections. Larger randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are required to confirm durability and clinical relevance. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2100052452.

item.title: Frontal Low-Frequency Electroencephalographic Coherence in Bipolar Disorder: A Covariate-Controlled Secondary Analysis of a Public Resting-State EEG Feature Dataset.
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
ObjectiveTo test whether bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with predefined frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp electroencephalography (EEG) coherence differences relative to healthy controls (HC), depressive disorder (DD), and schizophrenia (SZ) in a covariate-controlled reanalysis of a public resting-state EEG feature dataset.MethodsThe covariate-complete sample included 472 participants (93 HC, 66 BD, 196 DD, and 117 SZ). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for age, sex, education, and intelligence quotient (IQ). Primary outcomes were predefined frontal/frontopolar delta, theta, and combined delta-theta coherence means. Electrode-pair, regional, all-frequency, distributional, global-reference, frontopolar, and age sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.ResultsBD had higher adjusted coherence than all comparison groups across the three primary measures (partial η2 = .037-.040); Holm-adjusted BD-HC, BD-DD, and BD-SZ contrasts were significant for each measure. Features surviving false discovery rate correction were concentrated in the delta and theta bands. Findings were robust to distributional, outlier, and global-coherence analyses, but effects were strongest in frontopolar pairs and attenuated as anterior electrodes were excluded.ConclusionsBD showed higher covariate-adjusted frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp coherence than HC within this dataset. Differences from DD and SZ were smaller and concentrated in frontopolar pairs susceptible to ocular artifacts. Because only scalp-level coherence features were available and participant-level artifact-rejection data were unavailable, the findings do not establish a diagnostic biomarker, diagnostic specificity, or source-level mechanism. Artifact-controlled replication is required.

item.title: MAMBAxBrain: A multi-task neural framework linking brain functional dynamics to individual fingerprints, cognitive and disease states.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) contains rich individual, cognitive, and pathological information, yet no universal model exists for multi-task modeling of these dimensions. Here, we introduce MAMBAxBrain, a multi-task neural framework that integrates Mamba architecture with functional connectivity analysis to jointly model the temporal dynamics and spatial coordination of neural activity. MAMBAxBrain achieves high accuracy across four distinct fMRI objectives, including brain fingerprinting, cognitive task decoding, reaction time prediction, and schizophrenia classification, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods with robust cross-session generalization. Interpretability analyses show that each task engages distinct, biologically plausible circuitry: from higher-order association cortex for identity to subcortical-motor loops for reaction time and disrupted control-sensory connectivity for schizophrenia. These findings inform a longstanding debate: rather than operating through wholly separate or entirely shared systems, the brain preferentially recruits task-specific circuits while retaining common representational structure across functions.

item.title: Hidden Drowsiness in Wakefulness: Differences in Resting-State EEG Profiles in Natural Short Sleepers Versus Recommended Length Sleepers.
item.description:
Journal of sleep research
Chronic insufficient sleep affects cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous systems and is linked to cognitive decline and increased mortality. Among habitual short sleepers, a subgroup known as natural short sleepers (NSS) report sleeping ≤ 6 h per night without experiencing subjective daytime dysfunction. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective markers of alertness raise questions about their true cognitive state. NSS have been described as high in behavioural activation, a phenotype overlapping with ADHD and mania in which dysregulation of resting-state brain arousal has been well documented. Despite these parallels, few studies have investigated the neurophysiological features of NSS. The current study examined resting-state EEG in NSS and recommended-length sleepers (RLS) during eyes-open conditions. Results showed that NSS exhibited significantly higher global alpha power and regionally steeper aperiodic exponents, particularly in occipital areas, both markers of increased drowsiness. Although global exponent values did not differ significantly, a significant Group × Region interaction was observed and NSS showed a trend toward increasing aperiodic exponents over time, suggesting less stable wakefulness under low-stimulation conditions. These findings point to subtle neurophysiological differences in NSS, raising the possibility that their perceived resilience to short sleep may mask underlying drowsiness.

item.title: Depressive symptoms moderate daily anticipated and momentary emotion dynamics and associate with complex brain network topology: Resting-state EEG and ecological momentary assessment evidence.
item.description:
Psychological medicine
Background The dynamic linkage between anticipated and momentary emotion is a core daily regulatory process, yet the psychopathological and neurophysiological mechanisms disrupting this linkage in depression remain unclear. By bridging macroscopic neural topology with microscopic behavioral dynamics, this study investigated the within-person dynamics of these emotions and their cross-level associations with depressive symptoms and brain network topology. Methods Integrating resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA; 3 assessments/day), we recruited 96 young adults. Minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was applied to characterize baseline brain network topology across multiple frequency bands. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) was employed to examine within-person dynamics and cross-level statistical moderation. Results Anticipated emotion prospectively predicted subsequent momentary positive emotion (β = .191) and inversely predicted momentary negative emotion (β = -.125). However, baseline depressive symptoms significantly moderated this prospective affective dynamic: Johnson-Neyman analyses identified empirical transition ranges (PHQ-9 scores 5.7-9.7; mild symptom range) beyond which the prospective emotional link attenuated to non-significance. Furthermore, topological metrics in the theta and delta bands exhibited indirect statistical associations with daily emotional dynamics via their cross-sectional relationship with baseline depressive symptoms. Conclusions An attenuated prospective association between positive anticipation and subsequent momentary emotional experience represents a key affective alteration in depressive distress. This daily emotional attenuation co-occurs with elevated depressive distress and is indirectly associated with a centralized topological organization in low-frequency resting-state brain networks. These findings provide novel neurophysiological indicators and highlight the critical window for ecological interventions before symptom severity reaches the moderate range.

item.title: The information architecture of the naturalistic human brain
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
How does the brain orchestrate its central currency, information, for complex adaptive cognition in the real world? Here we provide a comprehensive investigation into the spatiotemporal structure of qualitatively distinct modes of information dynamics in the human brain under ecological conditions. Applying a novel framework for information decomposition to fMRI data from individuals watching full-length feature films, we reveal a multidimensional large-scale information architecture, wherein different schemes for storing, transferring, and transforming representations occupy disjoint topographic and network profiles. Further, this architecture reveals a computational division of labour, with certain regions acting as generalists that support multiple information-processing schemes and others specialising in a few. We show how these interactions reconfigure over time, coalescing into a structured cycle synchronised by sensory input, whose elements are tuned to semantic kinematics. Finally, we replicate these findings in an independent, large-scale dataset. Together, we provide a formal and empirical foundation for understanding the principles that govern distributed computation in the human brain during everyday life.

item.title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex). Across 11 datasets (n=478), MONS captured anger and disgust but was dissociable from general negative affect and affective arousal. Notably, MONS did not predict perceived moral wrongness in conventional moral judgment paradigms, suggesting that moral outrage is not reducible to more cognitive moral evaluation. Findings provide a moral outrage neurofunctional model that delineates its relationship to other affective states and distinguishes it from traditional moral judgment.

item.title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, yet how interventions reorganise brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression using pre- and post-treatment resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from a double-blind randomised controlled trial ( NCT03429075 ). We compared two whole-brain modelling approaches: conventional signal-space modelling describing interactions between regional brain signals, and vortex-space modelling capturing interactions between evolving patterns of local synchronisation. This represents the first application of vortex-space modelling to a psychiatric disorder. Vortex space was more sensitive than signal space in most analyses, including distinguishing treatment-related brain states, relating baseline connectivity to clinical improvement and predicting response to escitalopram. Our results further revealed distinct patterns of reorganisation following the two interventions. Psilocybin produced widespread increases in vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced network modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable changes. Despite these differences, greater increases in brain turbulence (i.e., spatiotemporal variability in local synchronisation) were associated with greater symptom reduction in both treatments, with a significant post-treatment increase in responders. These findings suggest that psilocybin and escitalopram may reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways and yet share dynamical features associated with clinical improvement. Overall, vortex-space modelling offers a promising framework for characterising brain dynamics in depression and its successful treatment.

item.title: The Dual Nature of Syntactic Node Count: Facilitating and Inhibiting Sentence Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Neurolinguistic research on syntactic processing has used Node Count, the number of syntactic nodes assumed to be built at each word, to investigate how structure-building effort affects brain activity. However, several recent studies cast doubt on the presumed link between Node Count and processing effort; they observe negative correlations between Node Count and reading times. These facilitatory effects raise an alternative hypothesis: rather than reflecting structure-building effort, Node Count may index structure-mediated predictability. To test this hypothesis, we first relate Node Count to an information-theoretic measure of contextual support, the pointwise mutual information (PMI) between a word and its context. We then evaluate the relationship between Node Count and reading times from three large-scale naturalistic English datasets. For these analyses, we derive Node Count under three grammar formalisms (phrase-structure grammar, dependency grammar, and combinatory categorial grammar) and multiple parsing strategies. Variants whose count reflects integrative parsing steps correlate positively with PMI and show a dual behavioral profile: robust facilitation in immediate regions, consistent with structure-mediated predictability, and a delayed slowdown in spillover regions, most consistent with the cost of contextual semantic integration. The facilitatory effect explains reading-time variance beyond GPT-2 surprisal, indicating that Node Count has unique psycholinguistic value as an index of human prediction. These results highlight the role of structural representations in human language processing and underscore the need for a careful interpretation of the observed correlations between Node Count and brain activity in neurolinguistic studies.

item.title: Correspondence Between Structural and Functional Connectivity Within White Matter
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract White matter functional networks (WMFNs) derived from resting-state BOLD fluctuations have been identified across multiple datasets, but whether they correspond to coherent anatomical units defined by the underlying axonal architecture remains untested. Here we tested WM structural connectivity-functional connectivity (SC-FC) coupling directly by asking whether regions co-assigned to the same WMFN are preferentially linked by WM tracts. Using resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI from the Human Connectome Project 7T dataset (N = 161), we derived 11 WMFNs per session (after exclusion of one boundary network) via k-means clustering of voxel-level functional connectivity (FC), constructed structural connectivity (SC) using multi-shell multi-tissue constrained spherical deconvolution with anatomically constrained tractography, and quantified the correlation between SC and FC across within- and between-network edges. Within-network coupling was two to three times higher than between-network coupling in both sessions (Session 1: r within = 0.59 vs. r between = 0.20; Session 2: r within = 0.66 vs. r between = 0.28; p < 0.001). The increased coupling was also observed across subjects, in terms of survived matching of edge counts, and disappeared when network labels were permuted. Network-level coupling was heterogeneous and concentrated in projection pathways spanning the midbrain and medulla oblongata, with rank ordering of the six highest-coupling networks identical across sessions. These findings provide structural support that WMFNs are coherent anatomical-functional units and support reconceptualising WM as a structured contributor to the brain's functional architecture rather than a passive transmission medium.

item.title: Attention increases the spread of modality-invariant information across the cortex.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Attention shapes our perception by allowing us to focus on relevant stimuli that are selected for conscious processing. In this work we assessed to what degree attention influences the extraction of modality-invariant information, that is, information that is independent of the input stimulus modality. To this end, we analyze fMRI data of subjects viewing naturalistic images and reading short textual descriptions while paying attention to only one of the two modalities. Using cross-modality decoding, we found modality-invariant representations in a small area of the cortex even in the absence of attention, spreading to much larger regions when stimuli are attended. This work demonstrates how state-of-the-art decoding techniques on large-scale data can be used to expand our knowledge on how attention shapes specific high-level representations in the brain.

item.title: The diastole-systole transition as a regulatory window for heart-brain coupling in major depressive disorder: Evidence from cardiac phase-dependent 1/f slope and periodic neural dynamics.
item.description:
Psychiatry and clinical neurosciences
Background Cardiac rhythms dynamically modulate neural activity and information processing. Disruptions in heart-brain coupling (HBC) may contribute to affective dysregulation in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet their effects on periodic and aperiodic neural activity remain unclear. This study investigated cardiac cycle-dependent modulation of oscillatory and 1/f neural components in MDD. Methods Resting-state magnetoencephalography (MEG) and electrocardiography (ECG) were simultaneously recorded from 60 patients with MDD and 60 matched healthy controls. Patients underwent a 6-month follow-up, and remission status was assessed using the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17). The Spectral Parameterization Resolved in Time (SPRiNT) algorithm was used to separate periodic and aperiodic neural activity. Linear mixed-effects models and permutation-based statistics were applied to examine cardiac phase-dependent neural modulation and between-group differences. Results Cardiac phase modulated both oscillatory power and aperiodic 1/f dynamics. Compared with controls, patients with MDD exhibited attenuated steepening of the aperiodic 1/f spectrum in the left insula during the diastole-to-systole transition and a greater reduction in δ-band power in the left anterior cingulate cortex during late systole. In addition, patients with MDD showed earlier α-band peak activity in the posterior cingulate cortex. Exploratory longitudinal analyses showed an increase in left insular 1/f modulation within remitters, although the formal group × time interaction was not significant. Conclusions MDD is characterized by disrupted cardiac cycle-dependent neural dynamics involving both periodic and aperiodic activity. Altered insular aperiodic modulation may reflect impaired excitation-inhibition balance and abnormal heart-brain synchronization in depression, highlighting cardiac rhythms as potential state-dependent targets for closed-loop neuromodulation.

item.title: Deep Clustering of fMRI with Global-Local Feature Extraction for Functional Brain Activity Analysis.
item.description:
IEEE transactions on bio-medical engineering
Objective Clustering is essential for identifying patterns in data. In neuroscience, it is widely used on functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data to uncover brain activity patterns during cognitive tasks and rest. However, traditional methods like K-means struggle with the high dimensionality and temporal complexity of fMRI data, and often fail to capture spatial or contextual structures in image data, limiting their effectiveness. Methods To address these challenges, we propose a deep clustering model that leverages the complementary strengths of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and Masked Autoencoder (MAE) for comprehensive feature extraction. The SAE captures global features and reduces data dimensionality while preserving overall structure. In parallel, the MAE reconstructs masked input patches to learn local contextual features-temporal for sequential data like fMRI, and spatial for imagedata. The combination of global and local features yields a more informative representation of the data. These fused features are then fed into a Deep Embedded Clustering (DEC) module, which iteratively refines cluster centers and feature representations using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence loss, improving clustering accuracy and robust ness. Results Experimental results show that our model effectively identifies functional brain activity patterns in task based fMRI and differentiates hippocampal subregions in resting-state fMRI. Conclusion Overall, our approach offers a unified and versatile deep clustering framework capable of handling various data modalities, enabling more accurate and interpretable analysis in both neuroimaging and general high-dimensional data applications. Significance The proposed framework explicitly decomposes global and local feature learning, overcoming limitations of single path deep clustering methods and providing physiologically meaningful clustering patterns.

item.title: Reading the night between the epochs: continuous decoding of sleep microstructure.
item.description:
Sleep

item.title: Right-to-left shunt burden and altered white matter functional networks in stroke-free patients with patent foramen ovale.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) is a useful technique for investigating the functional organization of human brain networks. Nevertheless, most rsfMRI studies in patent foramen ovale (PFO) have focused on gray-matter connectivity or structural imaging, whereas white-matter functional networks remain poorly characterized. PFO has been hypothesized to expose the brain to recurrent right-to-left shunt (RLS)-related microembolic, vasoactive and hemodynamic stressors, but whether these stressors are associated with altered white-matter functional organization in patients without overt stroke is unclear. The current study used rsfMRI to evaluate white-matter functional networks in stroke-free PFO patients and healthy controls. In the PFO group, RLS severity and anatomical features were characterized using contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler and transesophageal echocardiography. Nine large-scale white-matter networks were identified by K-means clustering of voxel-wise white-matter functional connectivity. Evaluation of spontaneous oscillations and inter-network functional connectivity showed that PFO patients had widespread reductions in fast Fourier transform-derived band-averaged amplitude, mainly involving motor, occipital, cerebellar, deep and cingulum networks, and consistently reduced inferior frontal-to-fronto-temporal connectivity across frequency bands. Higher RLS grade was associated with lower white-matter amplitude in several networks, whereas PFO anatomical measurements showed no independent associations after multiple-comparison correction. Exploratory mediation analyses showed no significant indirect pathways after FDR correction. In this cross-sectional study, these findings suggest that RLS burden may be relevant to subclinical white-matter functional vulnerability in stroke-free PFO.

item.title: Distinct developmental organization of intrinsic brain dynamics supports different components of inhibitory control during adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescent inhibitory control develops within a changing organization of intrinsic brain activity, yet the signal properties and cortical systems associated with different control demands remain unclear. We studied 101 youths aged 8–18 years using brain entropy (BEN), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Voxelwise and seven-network models evaluated age associations and task-by-age interactions while adjusting for sex, head motion, and gray-matter anatomy. Spatially standardized ALFF showed age associations in somatomotor and salience/ventral-attention networks. Contextual control, assessed with the AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), showed the broadest age-dependent coupling: all four spatially standardized measures yielded voxelwise interactions surviving permutation-based cluster false discovery rate correction, and the frontoparietal BEN interaction survived network correction. Better action cancellation was associated with higher frontoparietal BEN without a corrected network age interaction. Independent cortical references further differentiated these patterns: raw BEN age-effect evidence was stronger toward association cortex, whereas the ALFF–AX-CPT age interaction was stronger toward sensorimotor cortex. Additional task interactions aligned with the second and third connectivity gradients. Core voxelwise AX-CPT findings persisted after age trimming. These findings link the differentiation of inhibitory-control demands to the developmental organization of complementary intrinsic signal properties across cortical systems, highlighting contextual control as a prominent locus of age-dependent brain–behavior coupling. Highlights Age shaped links between intrinsic brain activity and contextual control Contextual control showed age interactions across four resting-state measures Frontoparietal brain entropy related to contextual control and action cancellation Selected age and control effects followed distinct cortical organizing axes Core contextual-control interactions persisted after excluding age extremes

item.title: Neural correlates of individual differences in cognition: a behavioral performance, EEG, and MRI dataset
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability. The multi-indicator design supports latent-variable modeling of all major constructs alongside their structural, functional, and electrophysiological neural correlates. Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). Electroencephalography (EEG) data was collected during four resting-state blocks and during task performance (cognitive control and processing speed). High-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), multi-shell diffusion-weighted imaging using the SANDI protocol, and multi-band multi-echo functional MRI during rest and task-switching were acquired in a subset. Behavioral, EEG, and MRI data are accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository. All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.
